source: Walton, Reed, Macagno (2008) Argumentation Schemes
finding: The book is a compendium of 96 schemes. Each scheme is a premise-conclusion template plus a list of critical questions (CQs). The scheme is defeasible: the conclusion holds provisionally until a CQ gets a good answer against it. Read here through the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on informal logic, not the book.
numbers: 96 schemes in the compendium. Expert-opinion scheme has 6 CQs in the SEP wording: credibility of A, A is an authority in domain D, what A asserted, trustworthiness, consistency with other experts, evidence base.
quote: How credible is A? Is A an authority in domain D? Is T consistent with what other experts assert?
limits: Secondhand summary through a page-summarising tool; SEP gave no CQ lists for analogy or cause. Book itself not opened.
agent_relevance: Our S4 can hold a table scheme -> fixed CQ list, and code can pick the list once the scheme type is known.

source: Makula (2022) The Devil is in the Framework (comment on Mizrahi)
finding: Quotes Walton et al. (2008, p. 91) for the basic expert-opinion scheme: P1 E is an expert in domain S containing A; P2 E asserts A; C: A. Walton (2006, p. 750) lists six CQs as the gateway through which examination dialogue is filtered: Expertise, Field, Opinion, Trustworthiness, Consistency, Backup Evidence. Identifying the right CQ list matters more than the exact premise list.
numbers: Scheme: 2 premises + conclusion. CQs: 6 (Expertise, Field, Opinion, Trustworthiness, Consistency, Backup Evidence).
limits: Walton's own 2008 text not opened; this is Makula's quotation. Makula is a commentator on the Mizrahi debate.
agent_relevance: A direct, code-readable CQ list for the authority scheme: six named slots, each answerable yes, no or unknown.

source: Makula (2022) The Devil is in the Framework
finding: Mizrahi (2013) argued expert-opinion arguments are weak: the fact that E says p does not make p much likelier. Seidel (2014) gave five counter-arguments. Walton (2014) replied that Mizrahi used an oversimplified one-premise scheme and ignored the premises added by answering the CQs. Makula says the dispute is framework-dependent: if AEO means a bare unsupported opinion, the weakness claim is true but trivial.
numbers: Mizrahi (2013, p. 76) as quoted: expert opinions are only slightly more accurate than chance. Debate: Mizrahi 2013 vs Seidel 2014, Walton 2014, Hinton 2015, Liao.
quote: research on expertise shows that expert opinions are only slightly more accurate than chance
limits: Philosophical dispute, no new data here. The 'slightly better than chance' claim is Mizrahi's summary of expertise studies, not checked by us.
agent_relevance: The strength of an authority argument depends on which CQs were answered, not on the bare scheme. An S4 check must record CQ answers, not just the scheme label.

source: Mizrahi (2013) Why arguments from expert opinion are weak arguments (as cited by Makula 2022)
finding: Mizrahi's premise (2): the fact that E says p does not make p significantly more likely. His AEO is the bare form 'E says p, therefore p', with no evidence and no peer consensus. Under that definition every AEO is weak by construction.
numbers: No numbers recoverable from the secondary source.
limits: Not opened; the original and the expertise studies it cites were blocked (HTTP 403 or login redirect). Treat the empirical claim as unverified.
agent_relevance: Warns that a scheme with no CQ answers is a weak argument; supports requiring CQ answers before accepting a source claim.

source: Kock (2007) Is Practical Reasoning Presumptive? Informal Logic 27(1)
finding: Critique of the presumptive model. Walton's scheme lists give a burden-of-proof shift: a proponent uses a scheme and the opponent must raise CQs. Blair (2001) said the origin and classification of Walton's schemes are unexplained. Pinto (2001, 2003) said many CQs have only heuristic, not normative, force and cannot shift the burden back to the proponent.
numbers: No numbers. Example from Pinto: for argument from sign, the CQ 'Are there any other events that would more reliably account for the sign?' puts the burden on the respondent to name one.
quote: Walton's list of schemes seems to drop from out of the blue
limits: Philosophical critique, focused on practical reasoning. No data.
agent_relevance: A CQ is a prompt to look, not a proof of failure. Our code should treat an unanswered CQ as 'unchecked', and only a located counter-instance as failing.

source: Lumer (2022) critique of Walton's argumentation schemes, Informal Logic 42 (search listing only)
finding: A search summary describes Lumer as arguing from an epistemological standpoint that many of Walton's proposed schemes are fallacious or not epistemically valid. The paper itself was behind a bot check and was not read.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened. Only a search-engine description.
agent_relevance: Possible limit: some schemes may never be reliable enough to test by questions alone. Needs a real read before use.

source: Nussbaum, Dove, Slife, Kardash, Turgut & Vallett (2018) Using Critical Questions to Evaluate Written and Oral Arguments in an Undergraduate General Education Seminar
finding: Quasi-experiment: two seminar sections used argumentation vee diagrams with a critical-questions box (Walton 1996, argument from consequences); a third section used diagrams without it. Experimental students added more refutations tied to the CQs over time. The effect carried to an in-class essay without prompts, but not to a take-home course paper on whistleblowing.
numbers: 3 sections (2 with CQ box, 1 control). N not reported on the page I read.
limits: Abstract page only; quasi-experimental (no random assignment); one scheme (consequences); transfer partial.
agent_relevance: CQ prompts help humans generate counter-arguments but transfer is partial: the prompt must be present each time. Supports running the CQs by code every time, not relying on the model to remember them.

source: Oaksford & Hahn (2004) A Bayesian approach to the argument from ignorance, Canadian J. Exp. Psychology 58 (as described in Hahn & Oaksford 2006)
finding: Recast the textbook fallacy 'argument from ignorance' as a Bayesian inference. Their single experiment (two topics) found that positive arguments were rated more convincing than negative ones, that people were sensitive to amount of evidence (one versus 50 studies or tests), and to the prior belief of the audience, all as the Bayesian account predicts.
numbers: Amount of evidence: 1 vs 50 studies. Model condition: positive test validity beats negative when selectivity exceeds sensitivity and sensitivity + selectivity > 1 (at prior .5).
limits: Original not opened; details taken from the 2006 follow-up paper's description. Only two topics.
agent_relevance: Argument strength is graded, not binary. A scheme verdict can carry a number (evidence amount, source reliability, prior) instead of pass or fail.

source: Hahn & Oaksford (2006) How convinced should we be by negative evidence? Cognitive Science Society proceedings, Experiment 1
finding: Experiment 1 replicated all three effects of Oaksford & Hahn (2004) with new topics and a different manipulation (source reliability instead of study count). Positive beat negative, reliable source beat unreliable, high prior belief beat low prior.
numbers: N = 73 (Cardiff students and staff). 4 topics x 2 polarity x 2 reliability x 2 prior, within subjects. Polarity: positive m=4.53 vs negative m=4.27, F(1,72)=11.58, p=.001. Reliability: m=5.58 vs 3.21, F(1,72)=198.63, p<.0001. Prior belief: m=4.47 vs 4.32, F(1,72)=5.96.
limits: Student sample, 0-10 ratings, dialogue vignettes. Polarity and prior effects are small (0.26 and 0.15 points); source reliability is the large effect (2.4 points).
agent_relevance: Of the factors, source reliability moves judged strength most. For the authority scheme the CQs on trustworthiness and evidence matter more than the label.

source: Hahn & Oaksford (2006) How convinced should we be by negative evidence?, Experiment 2
finding: Experiment 2 tested four structural variants of negative evidence across four topics, each participant seeing one variant per topic (Latin square). Both negative cases were always weaker than straight positive evidence, yet the opposite-polarity case was still rated well above zero. It was not always weaker than the same-polarity case: it was significantly better for the library topic.
numbers: N = 72. Topic F(3,217)=35.55; variant F(3,217)=19.05; interaction F(9,217)=3.71 (all p<.0001). Opposite polarity vs 0: t(71)=9.16, m=3.36, SE=.37. Library topic: m=6.16 vs 4.0, t(34)=2.39, p<.05.
limits: Strength varied a lot by topic, so no single ranking of variants holds. Small student sample.
agent_relevance: Same scheme, different content, different strength: a per-scheme question list gives structure but not a fixed confidence. Keep verdicts topic-aware.

source: Harris, Hahn, Madsen & Hsu (2016) The appeal to expert opinion: quantitative support for a Bayesian network approach. Cognitive Science 40(6)
finding: Recasts the scheme-based account of expert-opinion arguments as a Bayesian network over expertise and trustworthiness. Two experiments: participants' quantitative convincingness ratings were broadly in line with the model's predictions.
numbers: Exact N and statistics not obtained: full text returned HTTP 403; the repository page shows the abstract only.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Treat the 'broadly in line' claim as unchecked.
agent_relevance: A formal reading of the authority CQs: expertise and reliability are probabilities that combine, so the six CQs could be scored and combined by code rather than just listed.

source: Feng & Hirst (2011) Classifying arguments by scheme. ACL
finding: First automatic classifier of Walton scheme type, on the Araucaria corpus. It used general features plus scheme-specific cue features (for example keywords such as for example, and cause patterns from WordNet). Strong on schemes with obvious cues, near chance on abstract ones.
numbers: One-against-others best accuracy: argument from example 90.6%, practical reasoning 90.8%, cause to effect just over 70%, consequences and verbal classification in the low 60s (baseline 50%; only 44 and 41 training instances). Pairwise accuracy up to 98%; consequences vs verbal classification only 64.0%. Adding the linked-versus-convergent 'type' feature raised pairwise accuracy by up to 22.6 points.
limits: Five most frequent schemes only; Araucaria reported no inter-annotator agreement; 2011 feature models; balanced pools at 50% baseline.
agent_relevance: Scheme identification (the step before the CQ list) is the weak link for abstract schemes. S4 should let the model name the scheme, check cues in code, and allow 'unclear' instead of forcing a type.

source: Visser, Lawrence, Reed, Wagemans & Walton (2021) Annotating Argument Schemes. Argumentation 35(1)
finding: Annotated the US2016 debate corpus with Walton's 60 main scheme types, using a scheme key and an Argument Type Identification Procedure. Agreement was substantial but some scheme pairs (practical reasoning vs argument from values) were hard to separate. Earlier scheme corpora had very low or unreported agreement.
numbers: Walton annotation: Cohen kappa 0.723 on a 10.2% sample of inference relations in US2016G1tv; 14 Default Inference cases. Wagemans typology: 505 inference relations, 85 Default. Cited earlier work: Musi et al. kappa 0.1 rising to 0.307 after training; Song et al. 0.364 to 0.848 on only 3 schemes.
limits: Trained annotators with a decision key; 60 of 96 schemes covered; the authors say the taxonomy is a developing system, not fixed.
agent_relevance: Humans agree on scheme type only moderately to substantially, even with a key. Expect model scheme labels to be noisy too; do not make a hard branch on one label.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2024) Critical Questions Generation: Motivation and Challenges
finding: Proposed the task of generating critical questions for argumentative text. Compared theory CQs (Walton templates instantiated on annotated arguments) with CQs from two LLMs. The sets are complementary: theory CQs ask about relations between premises, LLM CQs ask more about evidence and definitions. Only about a quarter of the valid LLM questions were in the theory lists.
numbers: Llama-2-13B and Zephyr-13B on 18 annotated texts. Relevant LLM CQs: 80% (Llama-2, query prompt) down to 30% (Zephyr, query+definition prompt). Of relevant and related LLM CQs, 64.05% (155) were valid. Final: 21 interventions, 129 theory CQs, 52 LLM CQs matching theory, 155 valid LLM-only CQs; only 28% of 495 candidate LLM CQs were relevant and valid; 25% (52 of 207) of valid LLM CQs were in the theory sets. Theory CQs: relations 27%, evidence 24%, exceptions 18%; LLM CQs: evidence 27%, relations 21%, consequences 17%, definitions 16%. Template-filling agreement 0.88 on 174 variables; 39.44% of instantiated questions needed manual editing.
limits: 2023-era 13B models, 21 final interventions, annotators' own validity rules. Adding the CQ definition to the prompt halved bad-reasoning errors but added non-specific questions.
agent_relevance: Fixed Walton CQ lists miss about three quarters of the questions humans judge valid. Use the fixed list for checks that code can run, and keep a free-form 'what else could fail' slot.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation: A Challenging Reasoning Task for LLMs (dataset and generation results)
finding: Built a benchmark of 220 real debate interventions with 4,976 labelled reference questions (Useful, Unhelpful, Invalid). In zero-shot tests, 11 LLMs reached at most 57% Useful questions on average. Task-specific shared-task systems did about 10 points better.
numbers: 220 interventions, average 738.4 characters, 3.1 schemes each. 4,976 questions: 60.91% Useful, 23.21% Unhelpful, 15.88% Invalid. Annotator kappa rose from 0.19 and 0.26 to 0.54 after reason-based labelling (250 questions per round). Benchmark averages: top claude-3.5-sonnet; best open-weights gemma-2-27b-it 54.03; others about 43.4 to 53.5.
limits: Zero-shot, no prompt tuning; usefulness is judged against annotator reference questions, so valid new questions count as misses; average of 3 runs with std up to about 6.
agent_relevance: Even strong models in 2025 get roughly half of their critical questions useful. A single-shot 'find the weaknesses' prompt is a weak S4 by itself.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation (evaluation of the judges)
finding: Asking an LLM to label whether a generated critical question is useful agreed with humans almost not at all. Only reference-matching judges reached moderate agreement. A 7B judge (Prometheus 2) followed the generator's own misreading of the text.
numbers: Cohen kappa with manual reference evaluation: claude_reference 0.57, gemma3_reference 0.44, STS 0.40; direct LLM labelling at most 0.1. Against fully hand-labelled data: STS 0.20, Claude 0.28, Gemma3 0.31. Claude-reference left the most questions not evaluable, Gemma3 the fewest. Qwen2.5 models and claude-3.5-sonnet showed low diversity (templated evidence questions); o4-mini most diverse.
limits: Judge models were claude-3.5-sonnet, Gemma3 and Prometheus 2 7B. Diversity by an automatic metric.
agent_relevance: Model judges of 'is this CQ useful' are near chance; this repeats the same-model-judge problem (G4, G5). Check CQs by code against counter-instances, not by a model's opinion.

source: Alicante team (2025) ELLIS Alicante at CQs-Gen 2025: LLM-based question generation and selection
finding: Won the shared task with two small open models: a Questioner makes candidate questions, a Judge picks 3. In their ablation on the test split, giving the schemes and their CQ templates in the prompt did not help on its own. The best result came from mixing questions made with and without schemes.
numbers: Test split 79 items (train 74, val 33). Questioner only (Llama 3.1 8B, 6 questions), Useful: 54.7% without schemes, 53.4% with schemes in one prompt, 46.0% with each scheme in its own prompt, 54.0% mixing. With Judge (Gemma 2 9B): 57.7%, 56.5%, 51.6%, and 62.4% for mixing. Four candidates per prompt (8 total) best on train: 59.3%. Best shared-task score after organisers' human labelling: 67.6.
limits: Small test set (79 items); automatic usefulness by similarity to references, with 27 to 34% of questions not evaluable; schemes were the gold labels, so the null result is not due to scheme-detection errors.
agent_relevance: Handing the model the right scheme and its CQ template gave no gain over plain prompting and sometimes hurt. This supports SCHEMA 4b doubt: scheme templates are not a free win. A judge step added 3 to 8 points, most when candidates were diverse.

source: Zhou, Saadat-Yazdi & Kokciyan (2025) DayDreamer at CQs-Gen 2025: Critical Questions through Argument Scheme Completion
finding: Three-step pipeline: extract the argument for each labelled scheme, generate CQs from Walton's templates, rank. On validation the plain baseline had the highest raw Useful rate; their pipeline mainly cut the Invalid and not-evaluable questions. Most Invalid questions came from four scheme labels not defined in Walton (2008), for which templates had to be substituted.
numbers: Validation Useful/Unhelpful/Invalid (%): baseline 72.04/13.80/3.94; direct prompting 56.81/12.19/10.22; conversational 62.90/13.08/1.79; plus scheme sort 65.41/13.26/1.25; plus ranking 68.28/12.01/3.76; final 72.22/8.78/2.87 (rest not evaluable). Test: 4th of 13 teams, 60 Helpful, 25 Unhelpful, 17 Invalid with GPT-4o-mini.
limits: Optimised on validation; the goal was to reduce Invalid questions, not raise Useful. The authors report that LLMs hallucinate when given more than two scheme templates at once.
agent_relevance: Give one scheme template at a time, in code. Wrong or invented templates make output worse.

source: Ruiz-Dolz & Lawrence (2025) An Explainable Framework for Misinformation Identification via Critical Question Answering
finding: Built NLAS-CQ: 4,000 GPT-generated scheme instances (20 schemes, 100 topics, 2 stances) validated by five experts down to 3,566; 1,794 instances across 10 schemes have answered CQs (4,687 CQs). Classifying the scheme is easy on textbook text but drops sharply on real dialogue. Answering CQs is much harder, and prompted LLMs say yes to most.
numbers: Valid instances 3,566 of 4,000 (89.1%). Scheme classification F1: random 4.6, SVM 83.0, RoBERTa-large 99.2 on textbook text; on 287 real-dialogue schemes (QT30), F1 about 32 for the 8-group model and 44.8 after fine-tuning on dialogue. CQ answering F1: RoBERTa 70.7, with context 73.94; GPT-4 63.5, with context 62.5; Mixtral-8x7B 28.7, with context 34.6. Generative models answered 53.3% of negative CQs affirmatively. Questions with more wrong than right answers: Analogy CQ1 and CQ3, Example CQ4; weak on Popular Practice CQ1 and Waste CQ2.
limits: Textbook arguments are LLM-generated; CQ labels simplified to binary; 3 runs; 2023-24 models. Some table columns were garbled in text extraction, so the dialogue figures are approximate.
agent_relevance: A model answering its own CQs leans toward yes. Analogy and example CQs are hardest because they need outside knowledge, so S4 should supply retrieved or computed evidence for them.

source: Singh, Pathak & Singh (2026) Fallacy Benchmarks Measure Scheme Recognition, Not Fallacy Detection
finding: Fallacy classifiers learn which scheme an argument uses, not whether it uses it correctly. When correct arguments built on the same scheme as a fallacy were added as negatives, the classifier flagged most of them as the fallacy. Wrong-scheme controls were labelled with their own scheme.
numbers: ModernBERT fine-tuned on CoCoLoFa flags 16.6% of native valid items but 58.9% of scheme-matched valid items; trained on Reddit, 5.7% rises to 62.0%. Wrong-scheme negatives were labelled as their own scheme 85.9% of the time and as the source fallacy 0.4%. Matched negatives were labelled as source type 40.9 points more often than wrong-scheme ones. 76.9% of misclassified fallacies landed on 'none' (95% CI 64.8-86.7). Human-confirmed valid subset: false-positive rate 56.6% (30 of 53) vs native 16.6%. Judge precision 93.1% (67 of 72), Gwet AC1 0.69. Released 655 + 738 CoCoLoFa and 387 + 389 Reddit items.
limits: Constructed negatives; the authors say rates are not deployment estimates. Main classifier is fine-tuned ModernBERT, with three zero-shot detectors as a check; 8 fallacy types, 2 corpora.
agent_relevance: Recognising the pattern is not judging it: a scheme match without CQ answers over-flags sound arguments. The CQ step must test the instance, not the type.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn & Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis (failure by dimension)
finding: Four-phase protocol: classify the scheme in a model's verdict justification, generate that scheme's CQs, have the model answer them, and score answers on Govier's criteria. Across nine frontier models and 200 MoralChoice items, failure concentrated on grounds and sufficiency, not relevance or acceptability. Failure tracked epistemic hedging, not length.
numbers: 6,778 judge-scored cells; judge agreement 89.6% on the binary failure call. Failure 18.2% of cells; Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Llama 3.3 account for 67.8% of failures. Sonnet 4.6: 51.1% global sufficiency and 22.5% local grounds; Llama 3.3: 46.9% local grounds, 29.8% global sufficiency. Relevance failures under 0.5% on every model. Low-grounds vs high-grounds answers: median 738 vs 767 words. Commitment stability correlates with local grounds rho=0.27 and global sufficiency rho=0.49. Self-contradiction in 144 cells (2.1%).
limits: LLM judges score the cells; moral dilemmas have no ground truth; GPT-5.4's encrypted reasoning could not be scored; the hedging link is descriptive.
agent_relevance: Frontier models seldom fail CQs on relevance but do fail on grounds and sufficiency. Check those two by code (is a source cited, is it enough).

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn & Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis (scheme shift)
finding: The scheme a model used while reasoning often differs from the scheme in its later justification. Value-based practical reasoning dominates both tracks; justification shifts toward consequences (the authors' 'rhetorical recoding').
numbers: Value-based practical reasoning about 72% of reasoning-track (n=1,600) and 67% of justification-track (n=1,800) classifications; scheme differs between tracks on about 20% of dilemmas per model; VBPR retention 80.9% vs about 50% for other schemes. Reasoning track scores above justification on every Govier dimension except local relevance (3,182 paired observations, Wilcoxon).
limits: Eight-model panel (GPT-5.4 excluded from reasoning track). Retention table partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: A model's stated scheme is partly a presentation choice. Do not read a justification's scheme label as a record of how the answer was reached (consistent with G2).

source: Sarkadi, Garmendia, Mumford & Bench-Capon (2026) DeceptionAnalyser: structured deception analysis with argumentation schemes and LLMs
finding: Ten new deception schemes, each with premises and CQs, run in two stages: an LLM extracts the premises with a verbatim quote, then CQs are answered with a green, yellow or red rating. The authors say no scheme-level ground-truth corpus exists, so they measure only consistency across models and runs.
numbers: 10 LLMs x 10 runs per document, 800 premise/conclusion assessments. Clear fable (Fox and Crow): all elements green in 100 of 100, within-model stability and cross-model agreement both 1.00. Harder report (Operation Mincemeat): within-model stability 0.93-0.98, cross-model agreement 0.89-0.98; disagreement concentrated in the major premise (89% green) and two models.
limits: Consistency is not accuracy; two illustrative documents only; every premise assessment must include a verbatim excerpt, which discards ungrounded ones.
agent_relevance: Forcing a verbatim excerpt per premise is a code-checkable guardrail; cross-model disagreement marks the premise that deserves a closer look.

source: Hong, Xiao, Zhang & Chen (2024) ArgMed-Agents: Explainable Clinical Decision Reasoning with LLM Discussion via Argumentation Schemes
finding: A Generator proposes arguments under a clinical argumentation scheme, a Verifier attacks them using critical questions, and a symbolic solver (abstract argumentation) picks the acceptable set. It beat direct and chain-of-thought prompting on two medical QA sets.
numbers: 300 random items per set, zero-shot. MedQA, GPT-3.5: direct 52.7, CoT 48.0, ArgMed 62.1; GPT-4: 67.8, 71.4, 83.3. PubMedQA, GPT-3.5: 68.4, 71.5, 78.3; GPT-4: 72.9, 77.2, 81.6. In 63% of cases with no acceptable set, reasoning errors were identifiable; of those, 76% came from conflicting knowledge and 24% from insufficient knowledge.
limits: Single-team result, no repeats or intervals; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 era; baselines are direct and CoT only, not token-matched best-of-N or other multi-agent methods (G7). CoT fell below direct on MedQA with GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: A scheme-driven critique plus a code-side solver is one of few positive accuracy results (+10 to +16 points on MedQA over direct). Needs a token-matched baseline before we trust it.

source: Bezou-Vrakatseli et al. (eds.) (2023) Online Handbook of Argumentation for AI, Volume 4
finding: Search listing and front matter show a chapter proposing argument schemes and critical questions as a richer way to classify and instantiate arguments in ethical debate, for dialogue with AI. Results of the chapter were not read.
numbers: None.
limits: Only the preface was seen; chapter not read.
agent_relevance: Possible pointer to scheme instantiation by LLM in dialogue; low priority.

source: Modgil & Prakken (2014) The ASPIC+ framework for structured argumentation: a tutorial
finding: Per the SEP page (Prakken 2010): schemes can be treated as defeasible inference rules. Some CQs test premises, others test whether the rule applies in context, and acceptability is then computed in an abstract argumentation framework. The tutorial itself was not retrievable.
numbers: Tutorial cited 325 times (OpenAlex). No other numbers.
limits: Tutorial PDF returned a 404 or bot page; the description comes from the SEP entry only.
agent_relevance: A computational form: each CQ maps to an attack type (premise vs rule). Code can compute which arguments survive after CQ answers, as ArgMed does.

source: Walton, Reed & Macagno (2008) analogy and cause schemes (recalled, not opened)
finding: From memory, not opened this session: analogy CQs ask whether the two cases differ in relevant ways, whether the conclusion holds in the source case, and whether another similar case points the other way. Cause-to-effect CQs ask how strong the generalisation is, whether the cause occurred, and whether other factors interfere. The Calvo Figueras 2024 example (cause to effect) used the same two questions on generalisation strength and interfering factors.
numbers: None.
limits: Memory only plus one example read in the 2024 CQ paper. Verify against the book before coding.
agent_relevance: Draft S4 lists for the three schemes the field row names (authority, analogy, cause).
